messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 38
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Teacher
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 56

The patient is a 38-year-old European man, married, and works as a high school history teacher. He came to therapy about six months after the mugging, referred by his primary care doctor because of worsening sleep and irritability. Over the first few sessions, he began to tell the story in pieces, often stopping to check the clock or glance at the door.

The event happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. He had stayed late at school for parent-teacher conferences and was walking to his car in the faculty parking lot. The lot was poorly lit, and most other staff had already left. He remembers the sound of footsteps behind him—quick, deliberate—and then a voice, flat and close, telling him to give up his wallet and phone. He turned. There were two men, one with a knife. He handed over everything. They told him to get on the ground, and he did. One of them kicked him in the ribs. He remembers the pain, the gravel against his cheek, the sound of their shoes running away. He lay there for a few minutes, unable to move, until a janitor found him.

In the weeks after, he tried to return to normal. He went back to work within three days. But he found himself scanning the parking lot every time he left the building. He started parking under the brightest light, even if it meant walking farther. He began checking his rearview mirror obsessively while driving. At home, he would walk through every room before settling down for the night, looking for anything out of place. His wife noticed he stopped going on evening walks with her. He said he was tired. He was tired, but he was also afraid—afraid of the dark, of the sound of footsteps, of the way his heart hammered when a stranger walked too close behind him in the grocery store.

In the classroom, he feels different. He used to be animated, moving around the room while he taught. Now he stays near the front, back to the wall. He startles when a student drops a textbook. He began writing the day’s agenda on the board before students arrive, so he does not have to turn his back to them for too long. The noise of a crowded hallway between periods makes him irritable, almost jumpy. He snapped at a student last month for coming up behind him unexpectedly. He apologized later, but the guilt lingers.

He has nightmares most nights. In them, he is back on the gravel, but sometimes the men are his students, or his wife, or he is running and cannot move his legs. He wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat. His wife has started sleeping in the guest room because he thrashes. He feels a hollow shame about this—about how one brief, violent moment has reshaped his life so thoroughly.

He avoids the parking lot altogether now. He takes the bus to work, getting off two stops early and walking the long way, even in bad weather. He avoids walking alone anywhere. He stopped going to the gym because the locker room, with its echoes and sudden noises, feels unsafe. He does not go to bars or restaurants at night. On weekends, he stays home. His marriage is strained; his wife says he is not present, that he flinches when she touches him unexpectedly. He knows she is right, but he cannot seem to stop it.

He says he feels like a stranger in his own body. The world no longer feels safe, and he cannot remember what it felt like when it did. In session today, he sat with his back to the wall, watching the door. He talked about the mugging again, but this time he described the sound of his own breathing while he lay on the ground. He said, quietly, “I keep waiting for it to feel far away. It still feels like it happened yesterday.”
